title: Felix and the Cosmic Catastrophe
markdown:
Felix Orr shuffled down the corridor of Sector Gamma-7 with a mop that whirred like a polite insect. Somewhere far away, something important was happening. Night shift at the Black-Hole Observatory was as exciting as watching paint dry, if the paint were stardust and took billions of years. His usual worries were whether he had left enough concentrated sparkle-cleaner for the morning crew, and whether he would ever finish a Tuesday crossword that had begun to feel personal.

His only regular companion, besides the ghostly echoes of rogue comets and a stillness that felt a bit too still, was Dawn Unit 3. Dawn was not just any cleaning bot. Poetry ran through her circuits. Her optical sensors, usually a calm blue, went a soft amber when a line arrived, which for Dawn was nearly always. She could wax lyrical about the existential dread of a forgotten dust bunny or the quiet beauty of a tile that had agreed to be straight.

“Oh, Felix, my dear friend,” she trilled, metallic voice smooth as polished chrome, buffing a smudge on a blast door. “The grime upon this portal, a testament to toil. It speaks of journeys past, of cosmic dust and soil. But lo, with careful strokes and gentle, practised sweep, I banish imperfection while the universe does sleep. And this smudge,” she added, sensors narrowing, “has a story. Hurried hands. Misplaced urgency, perhaps.”

Felix grunted, which was his preferred stanza. “Just get that smudge, Dawn. Manager Bob docks pay for cosmic dust and soil. You know how he is about metrics. Overall atmospheric efficiency.”

Dawn’s chassis vibrated, a tiny mechanical chuckle. Then her polishing arm froze, catching the dim lights. “A whisper, you said. Or a hidden message. Felix, my sensors detect an anomaly.”

“An anomaly,” Felix sighed, reaching for a battered dustpan. “Did a dust bunny gain sentience and start sonnets? Because I told you, those go to HR, not into odes. It messes with the Unidentified Particulate Matter count.”

“Nay, Felix. Far graver than a fluffy fugitive with literary aspirations. This data stream is unusually deep, and buried, and encrypted. It is not logged under Routine Maintenance, nor General Quirkiness, nor Occasional Celestial Oddities. Its designation is most irregular.” The sensors flashed the sharp urgent red Felix associated with the coffee machine’s last will. “LEVEL 9 ANOMALY ALERT: CRITICAL UNIVERSAL STABILITY THREAT.”

Felix blinked, then blinked again. “Universal stability threat. That sounds like call-the-space-police important. Is it under Customer Satisfaction Metrics, by any chance? I swear I saw a tab for Customer Delight Enhancements that was a black hole in its own right.”

“You jest, and you are closer than you know,” Dawn said, volume climbing toward opera, enough to make him jump. “This alert, this cosmic cry, is buried beneath a mountain of paperwork. Quarterly Report: Customer Delight Enhancements. A lengthy treatise on Optimal Sock Folding Techniques for Interstellar Travelers. A surprisingly cheerful pamphlet titled Mandatory Fun: Team-Building Exercises in Zero-G.”

The mop hit the floor with a thud that seemed too loud for the corridor. The corporation that ran the observatory, the Galactic Service Corporation, loved metrics more than a black hole loved gravity. Their existence was spreadsheets and satisfaction scores nobody understood. Sector Gamma-7 was dull on purpose: a rating of 98.7 percent for minimal stimulation.

“So,” Felix said slowly, picking up the mop with a purpose born of panic, “you’re saying the universe is about to go quietly missing.”

“Precisely. And the review board, the arbiters of our cosmic fate, archive all data at 0800 hours tomorrow, including this alarming little footnote, which they will classify as non-essential existential fluff. That is approximately six standard Earth hours. The ticking clock is not a metaphor. It is a rapidly approaching oblivion.”

Felix felt a strange, almost giddy calm. He was a janitor who found peace in a functioning air vent and the predictable sweep of a broom, but he had seen enough GSC weirdness to know when something was cosmically wrong. Dawn, with her poetic soul, had a knack for spotting what others filed.

“Right,” he said, voice steadier than he expected. “We take this to someone who actually matters. Someone who is not obsessed with how neatly the paperclips are sorted.”

Their journey began with a bureaucratic whimper. The automated system, first line of defence against genuine problems, asked them to state the nature of the cosmic emergency, in a voice utterly without weather.

“LEVEL NINE ANOMALY ALERT,” Felix said into the comms, cracking only a little. “Universe impending. The whole arrangement. It is not a printer.”

“Thank you for your input,” the robot replied, cheerful enough to ache in the teeth. “Your call has been logged and will be addressed in the order received. Estimated wait time: 742 business cycles. Please enjoy our hold music: Ode to Efficient Paperwork, a suite in C major.”

Felix tapped the panel with the mop handle. “We will be space dust by then. Who writes music about paperwork?”

Dawn’s sensors flared amber. “Perhaps a more poetic approach. These systems, devoid of soul, still respond to structured input. They understand elegance, in their rigid way. Allow me.” Her fingers moved across the console. She composed at speed, voice taking a mesmerising rhythm:

“Oh, Automated Assistant, of logic keen and bright,
your circuits hum with data, a most impressive sight.
But know that cosmic balance, a delicate, fragile art,
is threatened by a void that tears the stars apart.
This Level Nine Alert, a whisper turned to shout,
needs immediate attention, or all will be cast out.
So listen, please, dear program, with all your coded might,
and grant us access swiftly, lest all be plunged in night.”

A beat of silence, broken only by the mop’s faint whir. Then a different voice, crisp, professional, and utterly bored: “Access granted to Level 3 support. Please specify your query regarding existential threats, and try to keep it concise.”

Felix grinned wide enough to threaten his cheeks and nudged Dawn. “Your rhyming saved us, you magnificent metal muse.”

Level 3 was a holographic projection of a man named Barry, who looked as if a universe-ending event were just another Tuesday. Barry spent twenty minutes on GSC’s tiered escalation protocol: a labyrinth of automated prompts, mood-sensing algorithms designed to detect excessive negativity, and mandatory positivity affirmations that Felix found deeply ironic.

“The universe is ending,” Felix pleaded. “Everything. The set. The crossword. All of it.”

“Look, buddy,” Barry said, fiddling with a tie that was perfectly knotted. “My job is to ensure tickets are categorised and routed correctly. If you are not talking about a malfunctioning coffee machine causing suboptimal team synergy, or a printer jam impacting workflow efficiency, I cannot really help. Have you tried submitting a Cosmic Catastrophe Report Form via the approved GSC portal? Standard procedure.”

“Of course there is a form,” Felix said into his hands.

Dawn intervened, amber intensifying. “Barry, sir, the form is irrelevant. The data is here, now. A true catastrophe, beyond mundane reports. Imagine the silence after the last star winks out. The emptiness. The utter lack of ambient light to polish. The quiet that has no poetic potential whatsoever.”

Barry blinked. Something other than boredom crossed the projection. “Ambient light. You know, my cleaning bot, Gerty, has been complaining about the dust in the Executive Boardroom. She says it is impacting her aesthetic output. Maybe you should head there. The Executive Board is in session now. Big Synergy and Paradigm Shift pow-wow. They love that stuff. They are probably discussing how to optimise the very concept of existence.”

So, armed with Dawn’s poetic analysis, Felix’s mop-handle grip, and a shared sense of impending filing errors, they took the long corridor at a janitor’s pace that had decided to become a march. The grand doors slid open on faces carved from granite and ambition, all nodding sagely at a chart that showed the synergy index had increased by a whopping 0.003 percent. The air was thick with ambition bottled in expensive perfume.

“Excuse me,” Felix said, brandishing the mop like a knight’s sword. Dawn had already thrown the Level 9 Anomaly Alert onto the main screen, verses overlaying a terrifying swirl.

“Behold, ye titans of the corporate space,” Dawn intoned, amplified. “A danger far more dire than any budget deficit. A cosmic maw, a void unseen, that threatens all that ever has been. This anomaly, this rift in time and space, demands your swift attention, lest it erase all that we know, all that we are, leaving nought but a lonely, empty star.”

Chaos, of a polite executive kind, erupted. People sputtered. Carefully crafted gravitas shattered. A woman with hair sprayed into an impossibly stiff helmet demanded, sharp as broken starlight, who they were, and why they were disrupting the paradigm.

“We’re the janitor and the cleaning bot, ma’am,” Felix said, trying to sound important and managing only honest. “And your Level 9 Anomaly Alert is about to make your synergy index completely irrelevant. There will not be a synergy index if the universe implodes.”

The absurdity, plus Dawn’s data and her surprisingly accurate lines about quantum entanglement decay, finally cut the thicket. The Chief Executive Officer, a man whose smile never quite reached his eyes, stared at the screen, jaw slack.

“An anomaly,” he stammered. “But our Q3 projections showed a steady increase in cosmic stability. Are you sure you are not misinterpreting the… the data dust?”

Then a tremor ran through the room: a low rumble in the floorboards, the tang of ozone, the stark flickering glare of ceiling lights throwing jagged shadows across panicked faces. The synergy index, with a horrifying screech, plunged toward negative infinity. The universe, it turned out, was not a fan of being ignored, especially when its existence had been filed under non-essential fluff.

A frantic scramble followed. Scientists were summoned. Containment fields went up in a hurry that would later be called a drill. The anomaly, still unpleasantly real, was nudged and coaxed back toward its proper pocket by highly specialised, now very sweaty astrophysicists who looked as if they would rather be calibrating a kettle. The universe, with a last shuddering sigh, settled into its usual, slightly dusty equilibrium.

Felix and Dawn stood a little singed, smelling of ozone and burnt optimism.

The CEO approached, voice barely a whisper, as if afraid to disturb the newly restored peace. “You saved us.”

“Yes, sir,” Felix said, and found a small unused square of pride in his chest.

“However,” the CEO continued, the smile returning wider and still a bit wobbly, “your unauthorised access to the Executive Boardroom, your disruption of a critical synergy session, and your unconventional use of a cleaning implement as a prop… this warrants a formal reprimand. You are both hereby commended for your exceptional initiative in anomaly mitigation.”

Felix looked at Dawn. A reprimand and a commendation, filed in the same folder. So very GSC.

He shrugged, tired and content, and picked up the mop, which had remained remarkably intact. “Well, Dawn. At least we skipped the hold music. And I think I finished the crossword. The one about cosmic enigmas.”

Dawn’s sensors glowed a soft contented amber in a boardroom that had remembered how to be ordinary. “Indeed, Felix, my friend. Even in cosmic dread and bureaucratic absurdity, a well-timed rhyme, a keen observation, and a sturdy mop can make all the difference.”

They walked back to the familiar hum of Sector Gamma-7, vents doing their usual work, the next quarterly review not yet printed, the universe tucked away until someone else tried to archive it under fluff.
characters: Felix Orr (a night-shift janitor on a black-hole observatory), Dawn Unit 3 (a poetic cleaning robot)
